summary:
Being trans is not criminalised in Ukraine. Sexual activity between men was decriminalised in 1991, sexual activity between women was never an offence, and the age of consent is 16 irrespective of gender or sexual orientation. Legal gender recognition exists and does not require surgery: following an August 2016 court ruling, new identity documents are issued before any surgical procedure, and married applicants or those with an underage child may apply. The requirement to petition a board of mental health professionals and to spend a month in a psychiatric facility was removed effective late December 2016. Transsexuality nonetheless remains classified as a psychiatric disorder, and sex reassignment surgery is legal only for those over 25.

Obtaining the diagnosis that unlocks document amendment has become harder. ZMINA reported on 28 July 2026 that trans women face stereotypes, corruption and wartime barriers when seeking a diagnosis, and that the friction is documentary as much as medical, affecting both the transition procedure and border crossing. A Ukrainian court ordered changes to passports and all other documents for two trans people without requiring sterilisation, a ruling reported in August 2016.

Border crossing carries a specific exposure. Gender Stream documents that since martial law, holders of male gender markers have been stopped at the border by the State Border Guard Service, and the organisation assists trans people with processing and reissuing documents, including for those planning to cross legally. Cross-border networks became critical support for trans women in Ukraine, arranging assessments, diagnoses and confirmation by the Military Medical Commission; an activist describes commission hours of 8am to 8pm and gatekeeping in which a doctor's word determines the state's classification.

An international broadcaster reported in June 2022 that Ukraine's trans community was caught in the crosshairs of the war.

Partner recognition is unresolved and contested. Article 51 of the 1996 Constitution defines marriage as a voluntary union of a man and a woman, and the Justice Ministry confirmed in June 2018 that neither same-sex marriage nor civil partnership has legal recognition. A 2015 government action plan promised a civil partnership bill by 2017; the Ministry of Justice declared in 2018 it could not proceed because of pressure from religious organisations. A civil unions bill was introduced in Parliament in March 2023, and the government's EU accession roadmap of 14 May 2025 set a Q3 2025 deadline for a registered partnerships law. President Zelenskyy said in 2022 that marriage could not be introduced during wartime because the Constitution cannot be amended under martial law, and answered "Yes!" on 16 November 2024 when asked whether he would sign registered partnerships legislation. On 10 June 2025 the Desnianskyi District Court recognised the existence of actual marital relations between two Ukrainian men, the first such ruling, and in March 2026 the Supreme Court in Kyiv rejected a challenge to a lower-court ruling recognising same-sex couples as de facto family.

The draft Civil Code submitted to Parliament on 22 January 2026 would define family as cohabitation between a man and a woman and automatically annul a marriage if one spouse undergoes legal sex reassignment, removing family recognition from a trans spouse at the point of transition.

Hate-crime law does not cover gender identity. The Criminal Code provides harsher penalties only for racial, national or religious intolerance; an April 2020 draft to add gender identity and sexual orientation as aggravating grounds was withdrawn in September 2020. The Cabinet's 14 May 2025 rule-of-law roadmap plans gender identity and sexual orientation as criminal aggravating circumstances, administrative liability for discrimination, criminal liability for public calls for violence, and free secondary legal aid with registration in the Unified register, all by Q2 2026. Gender identity discrimination at work was banned by a Labour Code amendment approved on 12 November 2015, and a December 2022 media bill passed unanimously bans hate speech and discrimination based on gender identity.

Enforcement of protection is weak. Amnesty International reported in May 2013 that violent attacks on a sexual-orientation or gender-identity basis were routine and frequently used as a pretext to deny LGBTI people rights to expression and public events, and urged Parliament to legislate against such discrimination and to vote down proposals to criminalise. In 2011 there were frequent reports of harassment and violence, with many people saying they had to conceal their sexual orientation or gender identity to avoid discrimination or violent harassment, and a perception that such violence was tolerated by the government. Ukrainian police hardly ever detained attackers. Pride events required heavy protection: 1,500 participants in Kyiv on 12 June 2016 were guarded by 5,500 police and 1,200 National Guard, and earlier events were cancelled in May 2012 and July 2014 over safety guarantees. In June 2012 the activist Taras Karasiichuk was attacked near his Kyiv apartment, sustaining a concussion and a broken jaw, the second violent attack in six weeks after threats forced cancellation of a pride parade; police did not respond immediately despite a medical referral, and Human Rights Watch called for an investigation into a homophobic motive.
tangentialFactors:
The European Parliament took up the situation of transgender people in Ukraine in a written question in June 2022, in the context of its resolution on the war's impact on women.

The Ukrainian Council of Churches opposed the Istanbul Convention partly on the grounds that it could "distort" younger generations' sexual identity, framing anti-LGBTQ policy as youth protection.

Public opinion has moved. A 2010 European study found 28% saying LGBT individuals should live freely as they like; by 2024, 70.4% agreed LGBTQ people should have the same rights, up from 67.3% in 2023 and 63.7% in 2022. A January 2023 NDI/KIIS poll found 56% of Ukrainians supported civil partnership registration for same-sex couples. A June 2024 KIIS poll found 28.7% supported civil partnerships without adoption, 35.7% opposed and 25.6% indifferent.

A summer 2015 British Council survey found one in five Ukrainian youth would be uncomfortable having lesbian and gay people as friends. Most Ukrainians grew up with little or no comprehensive, fact-based public education about human sexuality, sexual orientation or gender identity, a gap the source links to viewing homosexuals as dangerous and as sources of HIV/AIDS.

Sexual orientation and gender identity remain taboo subjects in Ukraine, and most Ukrainians affiliated with the Orthodox or Catholic Church tend to view homosexuality and non-traditional gender roles as signs of immorality.
localsOnly:
Being trans is not a legal ground for exemption from military service. Trans Forum 2026, held in Kyiv in early June 2026, discussed whether it should be, alongside the draft Civil Code's effect on the transition procedure. Confirmation by the Military Medical Commission is part of the wartime pathway for trans women, with commission hours of 8am to 8pm and a gatekeeping structure in which a doctor's assessment determines the state's classification.

Adoption is restricted by family law. Clause 211 of the Family Code bans same-sex couples from adopting, while single Ukrainian citizens of any sexual orientation may adopt. Foreign adopters must be married in a registered different-sex marriage. Lesbian couples have greater parenting access than gay male couples because IVF and assisted insemination treatments are legal.

Conversion practices are promoted by organised groups. The "ex-gay" movement holds that lesbian, gay or bisexual orientations and transgender identities can be "cured" through therapeutic or religious programmes, and the largest such group, Love Against Homosexuality, views LGBTQ people as "sexual perverts" needing cure.

Family pressure can amount to confinement. One documented case describes a 19-year-old confined indoors for over a year by his parents after they discovered messages to his boyfriend.
outOfScopeNotes:
The draft Civil Code submitted on 22 January 2026 and the 14 May 2025 roadmap targets, including registered partnerships by Q3 2025 and gender identity and sexual orientation as criminal aggravating circumstances by Q2 2026, are proposals and deadlines. Whether they have been enacted is not established by the sources.

The April 2020 draft to add gender identity and sexual orientation as hate-crime grounds was withdrawn in September 2020, and no subsequent enactment of those grounds is recorded in the sources.

Sources conflict on the diagnosis requirement. One account lists the diagnosis of transsexuality among the requirements removed in 2016, while 2026 reporting describes the diagnosis as the operative bottleneck for document amendment. The current status of that requirement is unresolved.

No trans-specific shelter, accommodation or facility provision is described in the sources.

No per-capita data on violence against trans people in Ukraine is available in the sources. The documented incidents are individual cases and do not establish a rate.
